content: Organic matter, also referred to as organic material, is defined as matter that originates from a recently living organism, is capable of undergoing decay, or is composed of organic compounds. The specific definition of organic matter can vary depending on the context in which it is being used. Soil Organic Matter Soil is a complex mixture that includes minerals, organic matter, and living organisms. The mineral component of soil is derived from the weathering of parent material, which consists of bedrock and the overlying sub-soil. The organic matter in soil primarily originates from plants and animals. For instance, in a forest ecosystem, leaf litter and woody debris accumulate on the forest floor. This material is often referred to as organic material. Once it decays to the extent that it is no longer recognizable, it is classified as soil organic matter. When organic matter further decomposes into stable humic substances that resist additional decomposition, it is termed humus. Therefore, soil organic matter encompasses all organic material in the soil, excluding undecayed material. Terminology The term soil organic matter lacks consistent usage across disciplines. In soil science, it may include both decaying materials and humic substances (humus). However, in fields such as agriculture and forestry, the term humus is sometimes used to describe both soil organic matter and humic substances. In soil science, the active component of soil organic matter is referred to as active humus, while the humic substances (or humus) are considered inactive humus. Once-Living Matter Organic matter can also refer to material that was once part of a living organism or was produced by a living organism. This definition aligns with the concept of biotic material and includes items such as a clam's shell or naturally produced urea, while excluding synthetically produced urea. Although this definition is useful for modeling nutrient flows, it is not practical for measuring the organic content of soil. Decay Organic matter can also be defined as material capable of decay, the product of decay (humus), or both. Typically, this matter consists of the remains of recently living organisms and may also include still-living organisms. Polymers and plastics, despite being organic compounds, are generally not considered organic material due to their resistance to decomposition. Similarly, a clam's shell, while biotic, is not considered organic matter under this definition because it does not decay. Organic Chemistry Measurements of organic matter often focus on organic compounds or carbon content, providing only an approximation of the amount of once-living or decomposed material. Some definitions of organic matter consider only the carbon content or organic compounds, without accounting for the origins or decomposition of the material. In this context, not all organic compounds are produced by living organisms, and not all remnants of living organisms qualify as organic matter. For example, a clam's shell, while biotic, contains little organic carbon and may not be considered organic matter. Conversely, urea is an organic compound that can be synthesized without biological activity. Vitalism The association of organic with living organisms originates from the now-discredited theory of vitalism, which posited that a special life force was required to create organic substances. This idea was first challenged in 1828 when Friedrich Wöhler successfully synthesized urea abiotically.
